summary: 12a opens by completing the synagogue/tzaraat discussion from 11b: the underlying dispute (R. Yehuda vs. Tanna Kama) about whether Jerusalem was divided among the tribes determines tzaraat law for city synagogues. A baraita then details which parts of the Temple precinct were in Judah's portion (the Temple Mount, chambers, and courtyards) and which in Benjamin's portion (the Ulam, Heikhal, and Holy of Holies) - noting that the Altar stood on a strip extending from Judah's portion into Benjamin's territory and so remained Judah's even though it sat inside Benjamin's land. On the Tanna Kama side, because Jerusalem was not divided, houses there cannot be rented out (and R. Elazar b. Tzadok adds that beds likewise may not be rented), so hosts instead take the hides of their guests' offerings in place of payment - from which Abaye derives the guest-etiquette of leaving the host the jug and the hide. The Gemara then asks separately whether village synagogues become impure with tzaraat, and a baraita derives from 'la'achuza' (for a possession) that house-tzaraat requires the land to have been conquered, divided among the tribes, divided further to the patrilineal families, and individually recognized by each owner - concluding from 'u-va asher lo ha-bayit' that only a house with clearly designated individual ownership is included, so there is in the end no difference between city and village synagogues. The daf then returns to the mishna: how is a replacement High Priest initiated if the original Cohen Gadol is disqualified? If before the tamid offering, he performs it in eight garments; proposals for initiating him mid-ceremony lead to a debate between Rav Adda and Abaye about whether a belt or the full set of eight garments (plus the tzinnora, a fork-like instrument) is required.

display.title: Cities vs. villages: was Jerusalem divided among the tribes?
display.oneLine: The underlying dispute about whether Jerusalem was divided among the tribes determines tzaraat law for city synagogues, and a baraita details which Temple areas fell in Judah's vs. Benjamin's portion.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara completes the synagogue-tzaraat discussion by identifying the underlying dispute: R. Yehuda holds Jerusalem was divided among the tribes (enabling private ownership and thus tzaraat); Tanna Kama holds it was not divided (no private ownership, so city synagogues may not receive tzaraat). A baraita elaborates on this by mapping specific Temple structures to either Judah's or Benjamin's portion: the Temple Mount, the chambers, and the courtyards were in Judah's portion, while the Ulam, Heikhal, and Holy of Holies were in Benjamin's portion. A strip of land extended out of Judah's portion into Benjamin's territory, and the Altar was built on that strip - so the Altar itself remained Judah's, even though it sat inside Benjamin's land. Benjamin longed daily to 'swallow' that strip, and for that longing he merited hosting the Shechina (the Holy of Holies, in his own portion). On the Tanna Kama side, because Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, its residents do not own their houses privately, so houses in Jerusalem may not be rented out; R. Elazar b. Tzadok extends this to say that beds likewise may not be rented there. Hosts therefore take the hides of their guests' sacrificial offerings as their due in place of rent, and from this Abaye derives the ordinary etiquette that a guest should leave his host the jug and the hide. The Gemara then asks separately whether village synagogues become impure with tzaraat: a baraita derives from 'la'achuza' that house-tzaraat requires conquest, tribal division, division to the patrilineal families, and individual recognition of ownership, and from 'u-va asher lo ha-bayit' that only a house with clearly designated individual ownership is included - concluding there is, after all, no difference between city and village synagogues.
display.whats: The tribal-geography discussion is not just historical curiosity - it has direct halakhic stakes for tzaraat of city buildings and carries theological weight about which tribe merited which sacred function. The Altar stood on a strip that remained Judah's even inside Benjamin's land; Benjamin's daily longing for that strip (not ownership of it) is what the Gemara says earned him the privilege of hosting the Shechina in his own portion. The same undivided-ownership premise also explains an everyday practice: because no one privately owns Jerusalem real estate, hosts cannot charge rent for lodging or beds, so they take their guests' sacrificial hides instead - and Abaye turns that arrangement into a general rule of polite guest conduct. The parallel village question shows that the real variable throughout is individual ownership, not city-versus-village geography.
display.hint: The Temple straddled two tribal portions. Ask yourself: why does the Gemara need to know exactly which structures fell in which tribe's land? The answer is usually halakhic (tzaraat, ownership) or theological (merit and reward).

learning.learnerQuestion: Was Jerusalem divided among the tribes, and why does the answer matter for halakha?
learning.coreTension: If Jerusalem was not divided (Tanna Kama), then land in Jerusalem is communally owned - and structures there cannot receive tzaraat, which requires private ownership. If it was divided (R. Yehuda), private owners exist and tzaraat applies. The dispute is not about history but about property law.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara identifies the two positions as a tannaitic dispute and then illustrates R. Yehuda's position with a baraita that specifically maps Temple structures to their tribal portions. The baraita presupposes division - it could not list which structure was 'in Judah's portion' if there were no division.
learning.resolution: The dispute remains unresolved in the Gemara, with both positions preserved. The baraita supports R. Yehuda's view implicitly. Practically, city synagogues' tzaraat status depends on which position is accepted.

takeaway.text: The status of Jerusalem as divided or undivided tribal territory is not a theological abstraction - it determines which buildings in the city are subject to property-based laws like tzaraat. Historical geography shapes contemporary halakha.

reasoningPattern.notes: Tannaitic dispute about historical fact (tribal division) generates different halakhic outcomes for property law

learning.ahaMoment: The Temple was simultaneously in two tribal territories. The Altar sat inside Benjamin's land but on a strip that stayed Judah's; the Ulam, Heikhal, and Holy of Holies were Benjamin's own portion. That means two tribes both 'owned' parts of the central Jewish sacred site - and this division has legal consequences that the Rabbis tracked carefully.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think tribal land division is irrelevant history. The connection to tzaraat and property law shows it is a live halakhic issue in Rabbinic literature.
learning.memoryAnchor: Altar on Judah's strip inside Benjamin's land; Ulam/Heikhal/Holy of Holies in Benjamin's own portion; Temple Mount/chambers/courtyards in Judah's. The Temple was split between two tribes - and that split has legal consequences.

argumentFlow.label: Was Jerusalem divided among the tribes?
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yehuda / Tanna Kama
argumentFlow.text: Tanna Kama: Jerusalem was not divided - collective ownership. R. Yehuda: it was divided - private owners exist. This determines tzaraat law for city synagogues.

argumentFlow.label: Baraita: Temple structures mapped to tribal portions
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: A baraita details which Temple areas were in Judah's portion (the Temple Mount, the chambers, the courtyards) and which in Benjamin's portion (the Ulam, Heikhal, and Holy of Holies). A strip extended from Judah's portion into Benjamin's territory, and the Altar was built on that strip - so the Altar remained Judah's even though it sat inside Benjamin's land. This presupposes R. Yehuda's position of division.

argumentFlow.label: Why Benjamin merited hosting the Shechina
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Benjamin the righteous was distressed daily, longing to 'swallow' (absorb into his own portion) the strip of Judah's land on which the Altar stood (proof-text: 'chofef alav kol hayom'). Because of that longing, Benjamin merited becoming host (ushpizchan) of the Divine Presence - the Holy of Holies, in his own portion (proof-text: 'u'vein ketefav shachen').

argumentFlow.label: Tanna Kama's side: houses and beds in Jerusalem cannot be rented; hosts take the hides
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: This Tanna (Tanna Kama, as cited below) holds Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes. Consequently, houses in Jerusalem may not be rented out, since they are not privately owned by their occupants; R. Elazar b. Tzadok extends this, saying that beds too may not be rented there for the same reason. Because the lodging itself cannot be charged as rent, hosts instead take the hides of their guests' consecrated offerings (such as the chagiga and simcha peace-offerings slaughtered and eaten there) by right, in place of payment. From this practice Abaye infers an everyday rule of etiquette: a guest should leave his host the jug (gulfa) and the hide (umashka) of the animal he ate in the host's house.

sourceRefs.note: Houses/beds not rentable in Jerusalem; hosts take the hides; Abaye's guest-etiquette inference

argumentFlow.label: Villages: a separate achuza derasha for house-tzaraat
argumentFlow.speaker: Baraita
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara asks separately whether synagogues in villages become impure with tzaraat. A baraita derives from 'la'achuza' (for a possession, Leviticus 14:34) that house-tzaraat requires the land to have been fully conquered; if it was conquered but not divided among the tribes, or divided among the tribes but not distributed to the patrilineal families, or distributed to the families but no individual recognizes his own portion, the status is unclear. The baraita then infers from 'u-va asher lo ha-bayit' (the one whose house it is will come, Leviticus 14:35) that only a house with clearly designated individual ownership is included, excluding houses not so designated. The Gemara concludes there is, after all, no difference between city and village synagogues on this score; the matter is resolved as already answered.

sourceRefs.note: Achuza derivation: conquest, tribal division, family division, individual recognition
Verse derivation and conclusion: no difference between cities and villages

misconceptions.misconception: The tribal geography of Jerusalem is purely historical and not relevant to halakha.
misconceptions.correction: It directly affects property law in Jerusalem, including which structures are subject to tzaraat and other ownership-based obligations.

visualizableElements.item: Temple map with tribal boundary line showing Judah/Benjamin division
List: Temple Mount/chambers/courtyards (Judah) vs. Ulam/Heikhal/Holy of Holies (Benjamin); the Altar sat on a strip that extended from Judah's portion into Benjamin's territory and remained Judah's

quizSeeds.question: According to the baraita, was the Altar in Benjamin's tribal portion?
quizSeeds.answer: No. The Altar stood on a strip of land that extended from Judah's portion into Benjamin's territory, so the Altar remained Judah's even though it sat inside Benjamin's land. The Ulam, Heikhal, and Holy of Holies were Benjamin's own portion.

quizSeeds.question: How does the tribal division question connect to the synagogue tzaraat dispute?
quizSeeds.answer: Tzaraat requires private ownership. If Jerusalem was divided (R. Yehuda), owners exist and tzaraat can apply to city synagogues. If not divided (Tanna Kama), collective ownership means no tzaraat for city synagogues.

quizSeeds.question: What four cumulative stages does the baraita derive from 'la'achuza' as necessary for a house to be susceptible to tzaraat, and what is the ultimate conclusion about city vs. village synagogues?
quizSeeds.answer: The land must have been conquered, divided among the tribes, divided further among the patrilineal families, and individually recognized by its specific owner. The baraita also derives from 'u-va asher lo ha-bayit' that only a house with clearly designated individual ownership is included. The Gemara concludes there is, after all, no difference between city and village synagogues - both avoid tzaraat where individual ownership is not established.

quizSeeds.question: Why can't houses (or beds, per R. Elazar b. Tzadok) in Jerusalem be rented out, and what do hosts take instead?
quizSeeds.answer: Because Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, residents have no private ownership of the lodging, so it cannot be charged as rent. Hosts instead take the hides of their guests' consecrated offerings (such as the chagiga and simcha peace-offerings) by right, in place of payment.

quizSeeds.question: What everyday guest-etiquette rule does Abaye derive from the practice of hosts taking their guests' sacrificial hides in Jerusalem?
quizSeeds.answer: That a guest should leave his host the jug (gulfa) and the hide (umashka) of the animal he ate in the host's house.

display.title: Initiating the replacement High Priest: belt and fork
display.oneLine: If the original High Priest is disqualified, how is his replacement initiated? Rav Adda proposes a belt; Abaye proposes eight garments plus a ritual fork (tzinnora).
display.shortSummary: The mishna returns: if the original Cohen Gadol is disqualified before performing the tamid, his replacement performs it in eight garments (the High Priest's vestments). The Gemara now asks: what initiates the replacement as a Cohen Gadol if the disqualification happens mid-ceremony? Rav Adda bar Ahavah proposes: just invest him with the priestly belt, and that single act is sufficient to initiate him as the replacement Cohen Gadol for purposes of the Yom Kippur service. Abaye counters: he needs to wear all eight High Priestly garments, and specifically also the tzinnora (a fork-like ritual instrument) as part of the investiture. Rav Pappa's answer begins at the end of the daf and continues into the next.
display.whats: This sugya addresses a Yom Kippur emergency scenario: what is the minimum required to transform a regular kohen into a functioning Cohen Gadol mid-ceremony? The dispute between Rav Adda (one garment suffices) and Abaye (needs eight plus instrument) reflects a deep question about whether investiture is a formal ceremony or can be reduced to its essential symbolic act.
display.hint: The belt is common to both the regular kohen and the Cohen Gadol. Maybe it is the specific High Priest belt that marks the difference. Or maybe investiture is all or nothing - you cannot be partially a Cohen Gadol.

learning.learnerQuestion: If the Cohen Gadol becomes disqualified on Yom Kippur, what does his replacement need to do to become the new Cohen Gadol?
learning.coreTension: The investiture of a Cohen Gadol is normally a formal weeklong process. In an emergency, the Gemara asks: what is the minimum that transforms a kohen into a Cohen Gadol? Can one garment do it? Does the full set of eight garments plus a ritual instrument need to be worn?
learning.coreMove: Rav Adda proposes that investing the replacement with the belt alone suffices - but the Gemara raises a difficulty: this only works on the view that the High Priest's everyday belt is identical to a common priest's belt (so the special Yom Kippur all-linen belt marks the distinction); on the view that they differ, both kohen and Cohen Gadol wear the same all-linen belt on Yom Kippur anyway, so the belt proves nothing. Abaye answers the difficulty: the replacement needs all eight garments plus the tzinnora, since turning the limb with the tzinnora is unambiguously valid service (a non-kohen who does so is liable to death per Rav Huna) regardless of which view of the belt is correct.
learning.resolution: Abaye's eight-garments-plus-tzinnora answer resolves the stated difficulty against Rav Adda's belt-alone position by proposing an act of investiture that is provably valid service under either view of the belt. Rav Pappa's answer, which continues the discussion, begins at the daf's end and continues on 12b.

takeaway.text: Investiture is both symbolic and functional. The dispute between Rav Adda and Abaye reflects two models: either one garment can represent the full status change (symbolic sufficiency), or the complete set of garments is required because each one contributes to the Cohen Gadol's halakhic standing (functional totality).

reasoningPattern.notes: Dispute about whether investiture can be reduced to its essential element or requires the full formal ceremony even in emergencies

learning.ahaMoment: The tzinnora (fork) is not one of the regular eight garments - it is an extra item Abaye adds. This suggests Abaye thinks even more than the standard eight is required, perhaps as an additional sign of emergency-appointment status.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may not understand why there is a question at all - can't they just put on the garments? The question is about what specifically is required and whether an abbreviated ceremony is valid when time is short.
learning.memoryAnchor: Rav Adda: one belt. Abaye: eight garments plus the fork (tzinnora). One man or everything all at once.

argumentFlow.label: Cohen Gadol disqualified before tamid - replacement performs in eight garments
argumentFlow.speaker: Mishna
argumentFlow.text: If the original Cohen Gadol is disqualified before performing the morning tamid, his replacement performs it in eight garments.

argumentFlow.label: What initiates the replacement mid-ceremony?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: If disqualification happens mid-ceremony, how is the replacement formally invested as Cohen Gadol? What is the minimum required to confer the status?

argumentFlow.label: Rav Adda: belt alone suffices
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Adda bar Ahavah
argumentFlow.text: Investing the replacement with the priestly belt is sufficient to confer Cohen Gadol status for the emergency replacement.

argumentFlow.label: Difficulty: the belt-answer works only on one view of the Cohen Gadol's everyday belt
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: This works out according to the view that the High Priest's everyday belt is the same as a common priest's belt (so the special all-linen Yom Kippur belt is what marks the distinction). But according to the view that the High Priest's everyday belt is not the same as a common priest's belt, what is there to say? On Yom Kippur both the regular kohen and the Cohen Gadol wear the identical all-linen belt anyway, so investing him with 'the belt' proves nothing.

sourceRefs.note: Difficulty on Rav Adda's position (continues the same Sefaria segment, vilnaLine 37-41)

argumentFlow.label: Abaye: eight garments plus tzinnora resolve the difficulty
argumentFlow.speaker: Abaye
argumentFlow.text: The replacement needs all eight High Priestly garments and additionally the tzinnora (a fork-like instrument) to be properly invested as the emergency Cohen Gadol. This answers the difficulty against Rav Adda: turning the sacrificial limb with the tzinnora is unambiguously valid 'service' (per Rav Huna, a non-kohen who performs it is liable to death), so the act of investiture is provable regardless of which view of the belt is correct.

misconceptions.misconception: Any kohen can substitute for the Cohen Gadol by just showing up.
misconceptions.correction: The replacement Cohen Gadol requires formal investiture - the dispute is about what the minimum investiture requires, but it is not optional.

Timeline: normal investiture (7 days) vs. emergency investiture (belt? / all eight garments?)

quizSeeds.question: What does Rav Adda bar Ahavah say is sufficient to invest a replacement Cohen Gadol?
quizSeeds.answer: Investing him with the priestly belt (avnet) alone is sufficient.

quizSeeds.question: What does Abaye require for the emergency investiture of a replacement Cohen Gadol?
quizSeeds.answer: All eight High Priestly garments plus the tzinnora (a fork-like ritual instrument).

glossary.en: The Chamber of Hewn Stone; the Sanhedrin's seat in the Temple complex, located in Judah's tribal portion.
The priestly belt; worn by both regular kohanim and the Cohen Gadol. Rav Adda holds it alone can invest a replacement Cohen Gadol.
A fork-like ritual instrument; Abaye holds this is part of the emergency investiture for a replacement Cohen Gadol.
The eight garments of the High Priest; the full investiture set required for regular Temple service.

rashiTranslations.en: 'Of cities' - for it is a place of markets, and people gather there from many places, and it
is made for all who come to pray, and it has no designated owners. 'of villages' - all
its owners are known, and it is like the house of partners. 'and Jerusalem does not become impure
with plagues' - for they have no holding in it; he holds it was not divided to the tribe of Judah and Benjamin;
rather, all the tribes are equal in it. 'I have not
heard' - he holds it was divided among the tribes.
'except the place of the Temple alone' - for when
David bought the threshing floor from Aravnah the Jebusite, he collected
the money from every single tribe, as we say
in the Sifrei and in Shechitat Kodashim [Zevachim 116b].
'About what do they disagree' - Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.
'The Temple Mount, the chambers, and the courtyards' - the
eastern side: the width of the Temple Mount, the whole women's courtyard,
and the whole Israelites' courtyard, plus eleven amot
of the place where the priests' feet tread,
beyond the feet of the Israelites, and there the altar
begins; from there and westward is in the portion of
Benjamin, except that at the place of the altar's base
a strip goes out from the portion of Judah
and enters at the southeastern corner.
'Chofef' - like a person who scratches himself because
he does not attain his desire; it is the language of the Nazirite ('he shall not
rub his head') (Nazir daf 42a). 'ushpizchan' -
that the Ark was placed in his portion. 'and this
tanna' - the one cited below, holds it was not divided,
and this is the tannaitic dispute. 'hides of consecrated offerings' - of
the chagiga and simcha peace-offerings that festival pilgrims
slaughter and eat there. 'gulfa' - a jug
of earthenware. 'umashka' - the hide of the animal
that he slaughters and eats in the host's house.
'La'achuza' - regarding plagues it is written (Leviticus 14):
'which I give to you as a holding,' for a house of
holding. 'to the fathers' houses' - to the families.
'and no single one recognizes' - that they did not divide
the family's holding among the individual men. 'as we answered
at the outset' - that it has a dwelling in it. 'it is obvious: if
there occurred' - a disqualification, in the High Priest, on Yom Kippur,
before the morning tamid: 'they initiate him' -
the one who serves in his place - 'with the morning tamid,'
that he perform the morning tamid in the eight
garments and thus be initiated into the High Priesthood
before the Yom Kippur service arrives.
'With what do they initiate him' - for the Yom Kippur service
that follows the tamid is in four
garments; and by what is he recognized as
High Priest at all, and where has he left the ranks of common priests,
so that the day's service be performed by a High
Priest? 'with the belt' - within those very four garments
there is a mark of High Priesthood, for the belt
of the High Priest in the Yom Kippur service is of fine linen,
as it is written (Leviticus 16): 'and he shall gird himself with a linen belt,'
and this one, until now, was accustomed to serve in one of
mixed kinds. 'this works out for the one who says the belt of the High
Priest' - of all the days of the year, was of
mixed kinds, as it is written: 'and the belt of twisted fine linen
and blue wool.' 'is the same as the belt of the common priest' - so there is no
distinction between their belts; there is a mark on Yom
Kippur in the belt, since the High Priest's belt changes on Yom Kippur
to be of fine linen. 'but according to the one who says' - below, that the High Priest's belt
all year round is not the same as the common priest's, for the common priest's is of fine linen, so their belts turn out
to be alike on Yom Kippur, and what mark of High Priesthood does this one have? 'Abaye
said' - before he begins the day's service, which is in garments alike to the common priest's,
he dons the eight garments and turns over, on the outer altar, one of the limbs of the tamid

with an iron fork; for it is an advancing of the service, since it is consumed faster on account of this turning, and it is a service, as per Rav Huna; and he thus turns out initiated into the High Priesthood
beforehand. 'with a tzinora' - with a fork. 'is liable to death' - because of 'and the stranger who comes near shall be put to death' (Numbers 18); evidently, advancing the service counts as service.
This ('his service') is the catchword anticipating 12b's opening comment.
